power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Voluntary perioral movements, including speech articulation, deliberate lip posturing, and postural stabilization during oral closure, require motor precision despite the absence of muscle spindles and proprioceptive receptors in perioral musculature.
The facial nerve is purely efferent, providing no direct sensory return.
How the motor system achieves stable control under these constraints has remained unresolved.
We propose the Orofacial Region as Integrated System (ORIS) model as a mechanistic candidate tailored to voluntary and automatic segmental perioral behaviors.

The model identifies cutaneous mechanoreception via the trigeminal nerve as the primary afferent channel for perioral motor stabilization and proposes that the controlled variable is the spatial equilibrium of dermal surface tension across the perioral sheet, monitored by slowly and fastadapting mechanoreceptors concentrated in the perioral region.
The orbicularis oris sphincter provides circumferential tensile stability against which directional muscles act, with the modiolus anguli oris serving as the primary force-transmission junction.
Three testable predictions follow from this architecture.
Clinical implications for facial motor rehabilitation are discussed.

The present framework concerns the perioral musculature (mimic muscles), defined here as the set of muscles surrounding and mechanically controlling the oral aperture, including primarily the orbicularis oris and its functional interactions with neighboring lower-face muscles involved in lip shaping, closure, and aperture regulation.

The account is deliberately limited to the lower face (with the possible addition of the frontalis): not all mimic muscles are alike, and the orbicularis oculi -governed largely by protective reflexes and under limited voluntary control -falls outside its scope.

These muscles participate in several partially overlapping functional domains requiring continuous sensorimotor stabilization: (1) voluntary fine-grained movements requiring online sensorimotor integration (e.g., lip protrusion, deliberate aperture modulation, speech articulation, voluntary facial expressions), (2) coordinative interactions with automatic orofacial behaviors mediated by partially distinct brainstem systems (e.g., swallowing, respiration, and mastication-related oral coordination), and (3) postural stabilization (maintenance of oral closure against mechanical, gravitational load or facial expression inhibition).

Despite their functional heterogeneity, these behaviors share a common computational requirement: real-time monitoring of perioral mechanics and online correction when actual tissue deformation deviates from the desired motor outcome.

The present formulation focuses primarily on the sensorimotor stabilization mechanisms supporting voluntary control of the lower face, while also considering their contribution to automatic and postural aspects of perioral behavior.

The model also encompasses involuntary and affective expressions at the level of their stabilization: once such an expression has been initiated, maintaining and modulating the resulting lower-face configuration is predicted to rely on the same mechanoreceptive feedback.
The model is not concerned with how these expressions are generated.
Among the motor behaviors the human face produces, voluntary perioral movements stand out for a genuinely puzzling reason.

People generate fine-grained modulations of mouth configuration during voluntary facial expression, deliberate posturing, and postural maintenance, i.e. movements requiring continuous adjustment of onset, trajectory, amplitude, and offset 1, 2 .
text.formatted: People generate fine-grained modulations of mouth configuration during voluntary facial expression, deliberate posturing, and postural maintenance, i.e. movements requiring continuous adjustment of onset, trajectory, amplitude, and offset <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">1,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2</ref> .

text.text: That precision arguably implies continuous closed-loop motor control, not unlike what underlies fine manual dexterity.
The control shows itself in two complementary ways.

First, under perturbation: when an unexpected load pulls the lower lip during the bilabial closure for /b/ or /p/, the lips compensate within tens of milliseconds to preserve the closure, and they do so without any view of the mouth 3 .
text.formatted: First, under perturbation: when an unexpected load pulls the lower lip during the bilabial closure for /b/ or /p/, the lips compensate within tens of milliseconds to preserve the closure, and they do so without any view of the mouth <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3</ref> .

text.text: Second, when the relevant feedback is removed: with a lower lip left fully mobile but numbed by dental anaesthesia, the lip seal leaks, saliva and food escape, and the lip or cheek is bitten inadvertently, markers of failures of online correction rather than of muscle force.
The anatomical substrate does not obviously support it.

In limb and trunk musculature, closedloop stabilization depends on muscle spindles, which encode length and velocity via group Ia and II afferents, and Golgi tendon organs reporting force via Ib fibers 4 .
text.formatted: In limb and trunk musculature, closedloop stabilization depends on muscle spindles, which encode length and velocity via group Ia and II afferents, and Golgi tendon organs reporting force via Ib fibers <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4</ref> .

text.text: These, together with joint and cutaneous afferents, give the central nervous system the state information it needs to update motor commands in real time 5 .
text.formatted: These, together with joint and cutaneous afferents, give the central nervous system the state information it needs to update motor commands in real time <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">5</ref> .

text.text: Eliminate that feedback, as in large-fiber sensory neuropathy, and interjoint coordination degrades substantially 6.
text.formatted: Eliminate that feedback, as in large-fiber sensory neuropathy, and interjoint coordination degrades substantially <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">6</ref>.

text.text: Notably, deafferented patients can partially compensate for proprioceptive loss through continuous visual monitoring of the moving limb ("visual proprioception") 7 .
text.formatted: Notably, deafferented patients can partially compensate for proprioceptive loss through continuous visual monitoring of the moving limb ("visual proprioception") <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">7</ref> .

text.text: An equivalent compensatory strategy is unavailable for perioral control: unlike a moving limb, one's own face lies outside the visual field during natural behavior, so ongoing perioral movements are not accessible to visual monitoring.
Beyond this lack of a visual fallback, the facial system differs from the limb case in three further respects that make extending the deafferentation framework problematic.
First, the primary mimic muscles appear largely devoid of classical proprioceptive receptors.

Muscle spindles are sparse or absent in the zygomaticus major, orbicularis oris, and orbicularis oculi [8] [9] [10] , and a recent cadaveric study confirms overall densities far below those of limb muscles, with the buccinator highest and the orbicularis oculi lowest 11 .
text.formatted: Muscle spindles are sparse or absent in the zygomaticus major, orbicularis oris, and orbicularis oculi <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10]</ref> , and a recent cadaveric study confirms overall densities far below those of limb muscles, with the buccinator highest and the orbicularis oculi lowest <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">11</ref> .

text.text: Golgi tendon organs are similarly absent or negligible.

Second, although trigeminal afferents clearly provide facial sensory information, the absence of a dedicated proprioceptive component within CN VII complicates the definition of a canonical facial motor feedback architecture 12, 13.
text.formatted: Second, although trigeminal afferents clearly provide facial sensory information, the absence of a dedicated proprioceptive component within CN VII complicates the definition of a canonical facial motor feedback architecture <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">12,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">13</ref>.

text.text: Third, facial muscles do not cross synovial joints.
They insert into the dermis or the superficial musculoaponeurotic system (SMAS), not onto bony processes across a joint cavity 14, 15 .
text.formatted: They insert into the dermis or the superficial musculoaponeurotic system (SMAS), not onto bony processes across a joint cavity <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">14,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">15</ref> .

text.text: Their mechanical effect is a deformation of a continuous compliant sheet, not a torque about a joint axis.
Joint-angle control frameworks are geometrically inapplicable here.

These three constraints together define what we call the "perioral voluntary motor control problem": the perioral motor system achieves motor precision that ordinarily requires proprioceptive or visual feedback, using an arrangement in which the standard afferent channels are either absent or unavailable.
Partial answers exist.

Cutaneous mechanoreceptors in facial skin respond to facial muscle contraction 16, 17 , and the facial and trigeminal nerves share multiple communicating branches that could route tactile signals toward motor centers 13 .
text.formatted: Cutaneous mechanoreceptors in facial skin respond to facial muscle contraction <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">16,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">17</ref> , and the facial and trigeminal nerves share multiple communicating branches that could route tactile signals toward motor centers <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">13</ref> .

text.text: These observations raise the possibility of cutaneous substitution for spindle proprioception, but no mechanistic architecture for such substitution has been specified.
That is what the ORIS model attempts, with the explicit understanding that what follows is a theoretically motivated candidate architecture, not an established account.
The cutaneous surface of the face is innervated by three trigeminal branches: V1 supplying the forehead and periocular region, V2 the cheek and upper lip, and V3 the lower lip, chin, and jaw.
This trigeminal innervation constitutes the principal candidate afferent channel for facial motor feedback, anatomically distinct from the efferent CN VII, which carries no sensory fibers.
Of the four classes of low-threshold mechanoreceptive afferents in human skin 18 , two are particularly relevant to motor stabilization.
text.formatted: Of the four classes of low-threshold mechanoreceptive afferents in human skin <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">18</ref> , two are particularly relevant to motor stabilization.

text.text: SA2 units (Ruffini endings) have diffuse receptive fields and respond preferentially to skin stretch and directional shear -they are the most likely candidates for encoding directional deformation of the perioral sheet during muscle contraction 16 .
text.formatted: SA2 units (Ruffini endings) have diffuse receptive fields and respond preferentially to skin stretch and directional shear -they are the most likely candidates for encoding directional deformation of the perioral sheet during muscle contraction <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">16</ref> .

text.text: FA1 units (Meissner corpuscles) encode the velocity and timing of dynamic skin displacement, suited to detecting expression onset and offset.

SA1 units (Merkel cells) provide spatial detail about static surface configuration, while FA2 (Pacinian) afferents are largely absent from the perioral and periocular regions, a structural gap that permits selective delivery of low-frequency vibrotactile stimulation to facial tissue without engaging the high-frequency channel 19, 20.
text.formatted: SA1 units (Merkel cells) provide spatial detail about static surface configuration, while FA2 (Pacinian) afferents are largely absent from the perioral and periocular regions, a structural gap that permits selective delivery of low-frequency vibrotactile stimulation to facial tissue without engaging the high-frequency channel <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">19,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">20</ref>.

text.text: Innervation density varies considerably across the face.

Whole-body density estimates indicate that the full face and lip region, spanning all three trigeminal divisions and covering roughly 675 cm² of skin, is innervated by approximately 19% of all cutaneous tactile afferent fibers, comparable in total fiber count to both hands combined 21 .
text.formatted: Whole-body density estimates indicate that the full face and lip region, spanning all three trigeminal divisions and covering roughly 675 cm² of skin, is innervated by approximately 19% of all cutaneous tactile afferent fibers, comparable in total fiber count to both hands combined <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">21</ref> .

text.text: Within the face, innervation density increases from the forehead and periocular region (V1: ~48 units/cm²) through the mid-face (V2: ~67 units/cm²) to the lower lip, chin, and jaw (V3: ~84 units/cm²), with the immediate perioral skin likely exhibiting locally higher densities still 21 (See heat map Figure 2).
text.formatted: Within the face, innervation density increases from the forehead and periocular region (V1: ~48 units/cm²) through the mid-face (V2: ~67 units/cm²) to the lower lip, chin, and jaw (V3: ~84 units/cm²), with the immediate perioral skin likely exhibiting locally higher densities still <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">21</ref> (See heat map Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2</ref>).

text.text: At the finest spatial scale, vibrotactile detection thresholds within the lip vermilion are significantly lower at midsagittal sites than at lateral sites 22, 23 , consistent with greater receptor density and receptive field overlap at the midline.
text.formatted: At the finest spatial scale, vibrotactile detection thresholds within the lip vermilion are significantly lower at midsagittal sites than at lateral sites <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">22,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">23</ref> , consistent with greater receptor density and receptive field overlap at the midline.

text.text: Three independent lines of evidence suggest these receptors respond to facial muscle contraction, not only external contact.

Nordin and Hagbarth 16 recorded from single afferents in the human infraorbital nerve and found that most slowly adapting units (interpreted as probable Ruffini corpuscles) responded to skin stretching and facial muscle contraction in the absence of any external stimulus, leading them to conclude these receptors may serve as proprioceptors for facial kinaesthesia.
text.formatted: Nordin and Hagbarth <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">16</ref> recorded from single afferents in the human infraorbital nerve and found that most slowly adapting units (interpreted as probable Ruffini corpuscles) responded to skin stretching and facial muscle contraction in the absence of any external stimulus, leading them to conclude these receptors may serve as proprioceptors for facial kinaesthesia.

text.text: Trulsson and Johansson 17 confirmed that facial skin afferents respond to deformations accompanying lip and jaw movement during speech and chewing.
text.formatted: Trulsson and Johansson <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">17</ref> confirmed that facial skin afferents respond to deformations accompanying lip and jaw movement during speech and chewing.

text.text: Cobo et al. 8 identified capsular sensory structures in the zygomaticus major and buccal muscles immunoreactive for ASIC2 and TRPV4, consistent with detecting contraction-induced tissue deformation.
text.formatted: Cobo et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">8</ref> identified capsular sensory structures in the zygomaticus major and buccal muscles immunoreactive for ASIC2 and TRPV4, consistent with detecting contraction-induced tissue deformation.

text.text: While these findings do not establish sufficiency, they provide strong evidence that the relevant sensory substrate is present and is activated by appropriate mechanical inputs.
The anatomical pathway from trigeminal afference to facial motor output runs through the communicating branches between CN V and CN VII documented by Cobo et al. 13 .
text.formatted: The anatomical pathway from trigeminal afference to facial motor output runs through the communicating branches between CN V and CN VII documented by Cobo et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">13</ref> .

text.text: These provide a multisynaptic substrate for trigeminal signals to reach the facial nucleus and cortical motor areas.
However, the pathway linking trigeminal input to the facial nerve may also rely on other central circuits.

Cortical facial motor control spans at least five areas -primary motor cortex, ventral lateral premotor cortex, supplementary motor area, and anterior and posterior cingulate -all receiving somatosensory trigeminal input via thalamo-cortical relays 24 .
text.formatted: Cortical facial motor control spans at least five areas -primary motor cortex, ventral lateral premotor cortex, supplementary motor area, and anterior and posterior cingulate -all receiving somatosensory trigeminal input via thalamo-cortical relays <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">24</ref> .

text.text: Two recent lines of neurophysiological evidence make this pathway more than anatomically plausible.

Pilurzi et al. 25 demonstrated, using afferent inhibition protocols, that cutaneous inputs from facial skin contribute to sensorimotor integration and plasticity in facial primary motor cortex; Ginatempo et al. 26 extended this work by showing short-and long-latency afferent inhibition in cranial muscles, indicating that trigeminal sensory inputs can modulate facial motor cortical output at latencies compatible with sensorimotor integration.
text.formatted: Pilurzi et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">25</ref> demonstrated, using afferent inhibition protocols, that cutaneous inputs from facial skin contribute to sensorimotor integration and plasticity in facial primary motor cortex; Ginatempo et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">26</ref> extended this work by showing short-and long-latency afferent inhibition in cranial muscles, indicating that trigeminal sensory inputs can modulate facial motor cortical output at latencies compatible with sensorimotor integration.

text.text: That said, whether these pathways carry functionally significant correction signals specifically during expression production -as opposed to speech or chewing, which were the test conditions in those studies -remains to be established 27 (see figure 1).
text.formatted: That said, whether these pathways carry functionally significant correction signals specifically during expression production -as opposed to speech or chewing, which were the test conditions in those studies -remains to be established <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">27</ref> (see figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: The controlled variable is the spatial distribution of surface tension across the perioral sheet, not joint position or muscle length.
Taken together, these findings establish that the facial sensory substrate is both anatomically present and functionally responsive to self-generated deformation.
Cutaneous afferents encode skin stretch and motion induced by muscle contraction.
Indeed, the trigemino-facial pathways operate at latencies compatible with online sensorimotor integration.
What remains unresolved is how these signals are organized and integrated.

In contrast to limb motor control, where well-defined models specify how proprioceptive and cutaneous feedback are integrated to estimate joint state and guide correction, there is no equivalent framework for the face, given that the insertion of most of its facial muscles is not on the bone substrate.

The system lacks canonical state variables (joint angles, muscle lengths), and yet it is capable of achieving stable, precise, and rapidly modulated configurations of a mechanically continuous tissue.
The critical question, therefore, is not whether facial sensory feedback exists, but what variable it informs and how it is integrated to control expression.
Current evidence demonstrates activation of the substrate, but does not specify the controlled quantity, the structure of the feedback loop, or the level at which correction is computed.
In other words, the field lacks a mechanistic model linking trigeminal sensory input to the control of facial motor output.
Here we propose the ORIS model, which addresses this gap by redefining the controlled variable and the architecture of facial motor control.
Before specifying the model, we delimit its scope.

ORIS concerns the sensorimotor stabilization of ongoing perioral movements, not the processes by which movements are selected or initiated; a posed expression, for instance, involves a volitional decision that the model does not attempt to explain, and enters the account only once initiated, at the point where the resulting configuration must be held and corrected.
The absence of an explicit control model for facial motor behavior reflects a fundamental mismatch between classical motor control frameworks and the physical structure of the face.

Existing models are built for articulated systems with discrete degrees of freedom, such as the limbs, where state variables such as joint angles or muscle lengths can be defined and precisely assessed.
The face, by contrast, is a deformable, mechanically continuous sheet, lacking joints and fixed reference points.

It is important to note that the mandible and its masticatory muscles (e.g., masseter) are a partial exception: they act across the temporomandibular joint and receive proprioceptive input via the trigeminal mesencephalic nucleus.
But masticatory muscles are not muscles of facial expression, are not innervated by CN VII, and fall outside the motor problem defined here.

This implies that facial motor control cannot be understood as a reduced version of limb control, but requires a different principle, one operating on distributed mechanical fields rather than discrete kinematic variables.
Critically, this field is not uniform.
Facial muscle insertions converge onto specific anatomical nodes, most prominently the modiolus, where multiple force vectors interact and are redistributed across the perioral sheet (see Figure 2).

text.text: These sites constitute localized hubs of mechanical tension, where small changes in muscle activation can produce large, spatially extended effects.

Here we propose a new model, ORIS, where the controlled variable is the spatial distribution of surface tension across the perioral sheet, structured around these convergence points, in particular the modiolus.
In this framework, trigeminal afferents signal local deformation, and motor commands act to stabilize or reshape a global tension field.
The ORIS model formalizes this account, providing a functional neuroanatomical architecture dynamically linking sensory feedback to the control of facial motor output.
Not all facial muscles contribute equally to surface tension control.
The orbicularis oris is sphincteric: it encircles the oral orifice with circumferential fiber geometry.

Sphincteric contraction reduces orifice perimeter and generates centripetal tension in all radial directions simultaneously, making this muscle a natural tensile stabilizer -a baseline against which directional muscles act.
That mechanical role follows directly from sphincteric fiber geometry.
The further inference -that the orbicularis oris serves as the primary reference hub for surface tension control in the perioral region -is a model claim requiring experimental confirmation.

The ORIS model is formulated primarily for the perioral motor system, including the orbicularis oris, modiolus, and associated directional muscles (e.g., zygomaticus major, risorius, depressor anguli oris, levator labii superioris, and buccinator), treated as a functionally integrated lower-face network.

This focus reflects the relative anatomical and neurophysiological tractability of the perioral region, where trigeminal-facial sensorimotor interactions, dynamic aperture control, and mechanically coupled muscle actions can be studied within a coherent behavioral framework encompassing voluntary facial expression, speech articulation, feeding-related coordination, and oral postural stabilization.

The present model does not exclude the possibility that similar force-balance and sensorimotor stabilization principles may apply to other circular facial systems, particularly the periocular region, where the orbicularis oculi also exhibits distributed insertions and coordinated aperture regulation.
However, the orbicularis oculi is not incorporated into the current formulation because its functional organization is substantially more heterogeneous.

In particular, the tarsal component is strongly constrained by automatic reflexive control (e.g., corneal and protective blink circuits), whereas the orbital component shows mixed voluntary and involuntary properties.
Moreover, the mechanical and sensorimotor interactions linking periocular structures to the perioral stabilization network remain insufficiently characterized.
Extension of the ORIS framework to periocular control, therefore, requires separate anatomical and functional analysis and is deferred to future work.
The predictions developed here apply specifically to the perioral system.

The oral hub (upper panel) shows the orbicularis oris acting as a sphincteric tensile stabilizer, with directional muscles (e.g., risorius) producing antagonistic force vectors converging at the modiolus -a serial arrangement operating on a deformable surface without proprioceptive or visual feedback.

The arm (lower panel) illustrates the classical limb architecture: parallel muscles acting on a joint-based system with discrete degrees of freedom, supported by spindle-based proprioception and eventually visual monitoring.

Limb control stabilizes joint kinematics through spindle-based proprioception and an active gamma motor system that continuously adjusts spindle sensitivity during voluntary movement, preventing the limb from reverting toward a fixed mechanical equilibrium.
By contrast, the facial motor system lacks an equivalent gamma mechanism.
Consequently, voluntary perioral configurations are transient deviations from a preferred resting configuration rather than stable alternative equilibrium states.
The ORIS model therefore proposes that facial motor control stabilizes a distributed surface tension field around this default mechanical configuration.
A critical feature of the perioral system is its asymmetric resting-state architecture.
The default configuration (mouth closed, lips approximated) represents the preferred mechanical state of the perioral apparatus rather than a neutral equilibrium.

This configuration emerges primarily from the elastic and viscoelastic properties of the lips and surrounding soft tissues, together with brainstem reflex organization that favours lip approximation when the system is perturbed, without requiring continuous tonic activity of the orbicularis oris at rest, which appears to be infrequent under normal resting conditions 31 .

Because these jaw-closing muscles lie outside the perioral system defined here (Section 3.1), the default tension field refers specifically to this low-activity perioral configuration.
Mouth-opening muscles, by contrast, are recruited mainly during voluntary or task-dependent behaviours rather than contributing to the default resting configuration.
Most voluntary perioral movements therefore represent departures from this preferred mechanical state.

Directional muscles reshape the perioral tension field away from its default configuration, while the circumferential geometry and passive mechanical properties of the orbicularis oris provide a stable tensile reference against which these deformations occur.
The ORIS model therefore treats the resting oral closure configuration as the default tension field from which voluntary deviations are monitored and corrected.

Unlike the limb motor system, which relies on spindle-based proprioception and γ-motoneuron regulation to support multiple stable postural configurations, the facial motor system lacks an equivalent γ-motor mechanism.
Consequently, voluntary perioral configurations are transient deviations from a preferred resting configuration rather than alternative equilibrium states.

Despite the absence of a dedicated proprioceptive nerve, this constitutes a plausible closed-loop architecture: efferent channel CN VII, candidate afferent channel CN V. Whether it operates with sufficient latency and precision for voluntary perioral movement is the central empirical question the predictions below address.
The model predicts that control precision and level scale with afferent uncertainty.
Under favorable conditions -intact mechanoreception, well-practiced voluntary movement, minimal perturbation -brainstem-level feedback via short-latency trigeminal-facial arcs may be sufficient 5 .

text.text: Two things can degrade this regime.
Afferent precision can drop through receptor adaptation or desensitization, weakening the error signal itself.

Alternatively, the target tension configuration may be underspecified when it must be constructed online, as in a deliberately posed expression, rather than being supplied by a well-practised motor program.
Whether an affective or limbic contribution also helps specify this target in spontaneous expression is an open question we return to below.

In either case the model predicts escalation to cortical control, with premotor cortex, supplementary motor area, and parietal somatosensory areas recruited to supplement degraded peripheral signals and to construct or hold the target through internal forward models 33.

Critically, their combined effect is integrated at the modiolus -the convergence node where the vector sum of all active insertions determines the resulting tension field.

Because the motor system monitors this resultant rather than individual muscle states, the computational load collapses: independent regulation of eight to twelve perioral muscles reduces to management of a single distributed quantity at a small number of high-density receptor sites (See Figure 4).

Posed expressions, decoupled from spontaneous emotional drive, may be less able to rely on a pre-specified target of the kind a well-practised, emotionally driven expression can provide, and may require greater explicit directional recruitment per unit of surface displacement.

The asymmetry between Duchenne and non-Duchenne smiles is consistent with this: posed smiles have faster onsets 34 , tend toward left-sided asymmetry where spontaneous smiles are more nearly symmetric 35 , and recruit the corticobulbar route rather than the subcortical limbic route that drives emotional expression 36, 37 .

text.text: This does not conflict with the model's feedback-dependence: the routes differ in what they supply at initiation, not in whether the movement is stabilized by afferent correction.

On this account, a well-practised, emotionally driven expression may carry a pre-specified target that allows stabilization largely at brainstem level, whereas a posed or volitional expression, lacking such a target, would construct it online and lean on the slower cortical arc (the escalation under uncertainty predicted in Section 3.4).

We present this as a hypothesis rather than an established mechanism: whether, and how, an affective state contributes to specifying the target tension configuration remains an open empirical question, and the Duchenne/non-Duchenne asymmetry noted above is consistent with it but does not establish it.
Direct energetic measurement has not been performed.
The predictions below are designed to be discriminable from both null models and from existing sensorimotor accounts.
Each prediction specifies the expected signature under the ORIS model and includes an explicit criterion for falsification.
The first prediction concerns the functional role of the perioral region.
More specifically, the orbicularis oris and adjacent perioral skin serve as the primary hub-level for feedback stabilization monitoring.

If this region provides critical sensory input for online correction, then selectively reducing mechanoreceptive sensitivity (for example through topical anesthesia or vibrotactile adaptation) should impair feedback without disrupting motor command generation.

Thus, under such conditions, we expect a preserved perioral displacement amplitude but an increase in trial-totrial kinematic variability, accompanied by a shift in EMG dynamics toward lower temporal frequencies, reflecting degraded high-frequency correction.

Conversely, a reduction in amplitude would point toward a more general motor impairment, while the absence of any measurable effect would argue against a functional role of cutaneous feedback during real-time control.
Critically, this prediction is spatially specific.

ORIS predicts that desensitization effects should be maximal at hub locations (particularly the orbicularis oris and the modiolus, where multiple muscle forces converge and are redistributed across the face) and weaker at non-hub sites such as the belly of the zygomaticus major.
Reducing sensitivity at a hub should therefore produce a larger increase in knematic variability than an equivalent manipulation elsewhere.
Absent such a dissociation, a more distributed feedback architecture would be favored over the hub-based organization that ORIS proposes.
External tension perturbation evokes distributed corrective responses.
A complementary prediction follows from the claim that the controlled variable is surface tension rather than position or muscle activation per se.

If facial motor control operates on a tension field, a controlled mechanical perturbation of the facial surface (for instance applying calibrated skin stretch near the modiolus during an ongoing expression) should elicit rapid corrective responses that oppose the perturbation.
Because the perioral sheet is mechanically coupled, these corrections should be distributed across multiple muscles rather than confined to the directly perturbed region.
Failure to observe corrective responses, or responses restricted to the perturbed site, would argue against tension-field regulation.

If a closed trigeminal-facial sensorimotor loop contributes to online facial motor control, brief mechanical displacement of upper lip skin during an ongoing voluntary perioral movement should elicit a temporally structured EMG response in orbicularis oris and associated perioral muscles.

An early short-latency component (approximately 20-40 ms) would be consistent with rapid trigemino-facial sensorimotor circuitry mediated at the brainstem level, whereas a later longlatency component (>60 ms) may reflect cortical sensorimotor re-engagement and corrective integration.

text.text: Importantly, the early response is not predicted to be uniformly excitatory, but may instead consist of mixed inhibitory and facilitatory modulation across different motor-unit populations, consistent with documented heterogeneity in human perioral short-latency reflex physiology 38.

text.text: Rapid compensatory responses to perioral perturbation have been described in speech motor control, including coordinated upper and lower lip muscle adjustments following mechanical loading during speech production 3 .

These compensatory responses occur despite the relative absence of classical muscle spindle architecture in mimetic musculature and are thought to depend predominantly on cutaneous and mucosal mechanoreceptive afferents.

More broadly, rapid sensorimotor corrective responses are well characterized in limb motor control systems 4 , although the facial system likely relies on distinct trigeminofacial mechanisms adapted to deformable softtissue control rather than canonical spindle-mediated stretch reflexes.

text.text: Comparative evidence further supports a distributed perioral coordination architecture.

In macaques, communicative facial behaviors show strong and selective coordination among perioral mimetic muscles, with orbicularis oris acting as a central coordinating hub during facial communication but not during ingestive behaviors 39 .

text.text: This organization is consistent with the force-balance architecture proposed by the present model.

A further prediction is that selective infraorbital nerve block should attenuate or abolish the early short-latency component while leaving later long-latency responses relatively preserved, thereby pharmacologically dissociating rapid trigemino-facial circuitry from later cortical sensorimotor processes.
If the early component remains unaffected by infraorbital blockade, the specific afferent pathway proposed by the model would require revision.

Conversely, if perioral perturbation elicits only a monophasic long-latency response, or if infraorbital blockade suppresses both temporal components equally, the proposed dual-loop brainstem-plus-cortical architecture would not be supported.

If ORIS correctly identifies voluntary perioral control as feedback-dependent and affective expression as pre-programmed, then selective disruption of perioral mechanoreception (e.g., via topical anesthesia of the infraorbital territory) should impair voluntary perioral movements (lip rounding on command, sustained protrusion, deliberate aperture modulation) while leaving the motor production of spontaneous affective expressions (smiling, grimacing) intact.
This dissociation is the most direct test of the model's foundational scope claim.

Disconfirmation: if perioral desensitization equally impairs voluntary and affective movements, the distinction between feedback-dependent and pre-programmed motor control is not supported, and the model's scope restriction requires revision.

Conversely, if voluntary movements are selectively impaired, ORIS predicts that the deficit should be maximal at hub locations (orbicularis oris, modiolus) and minimal at non-hub sites, replicating the spatial specificity pattern of Prediction 1 within a clinical paradigm.
>Implications
text.formatted: <head n="5." >Implications</head>

text.text: Peripheral facial palsy, facial motor apraxia, and developmental dyspraxia of speech are typically interpreted primarily as disorders of motor output or motor planning.

The ORIS model proposes a complementary deficit that may contribute substantially to impaired function across these conditions: disruption of the trigeminal-cutaneous feedback architecture supporting perioral motor stabilization.
In peripheral facial palsy, dysfunction of the orbicularis oris does not merely reduce movement amplitude.
It may also disrupt the deformation-dependent afferent signals that normally contribute to stabilization of the perioral tension field.
Recovery of voluntary movement amplitude may therefore fail to restore the dynamic correction mechanisms required for stable perioral control.

A related dissociation is frequently observed in bucco-facial apraxia and impaired voluntary facial mimicry: patients may retain relatively preserved spontaneous affective expressions while showing difficulty with commanded, imitative, or voluntarily configured perioral movements such as deliberate lip rounding, sustained protrusion, or precise lower-face shaping.
Classical interpretations attribute this dissociation primarily to separate limbic and cortical motor pathways.
The ORIS model instead suggests that different behavioral regimes rely to different degrees on online sensorimotor stabilization.
Highly flexible voluntary and imitative perioral behaviors may place greater demands on trigeminal-cutaneous feedback than more stereotyped affective expressions.

Within this framework, disruption of perioral sensorimotor integration -through trigeminal neuropathy, central lesion, developmental failure of sensorimotor coupling, or incomplete recovery after facial palsy -should degrade movement stability even when gross motor output remains structurally intact.

The model therefore predicts that affected patients may show: (1) elevated perioral vibrotactile thresholds, reflecting impaired afferent signaling; (2) abnormal reflex responses to perioral perturbation, consistent with disruption of rapid trigeminofacial stabilization pathways; and (3) preserved mean movement amplitude accompanied by increased kinematic variability during voluntary perioral movements, as predicted in Prediction 1.
This reinterpretation has potential therapeutic implications.

Rehabilitation strategies designed to restore or augment perioral mechanoreceptive feedback -including vibrotactile biofeedback, mirror-assisted sensorimotor training, or neuromuscular electrical stimulation protocols aimed at re-engaging afferent pathways rather than simply driving contraction 40 -may improve movement stability and speech intelligibility more effectively than motor-only interventions.

text.text: The ORIS model therefore provides a mechanistic rationale for sensory-motor integration approaches across a range of conditions involving impaired lower-face control, including developmental dyspraxia of speech, unilateral facial palsy with incomplete voluntary recovery, oral-motor dyspraxia following stroke or traumatic brain injury, and facial reanimation after Moebius syndrome smile surgery.
The ORIS model also bears on accounts of emotion recognition and sensorimotor simulation.

Classical facial-feedback accounts hold that facial motor activity contributes to emotion processing by feeding back into central affective systems 41 , but the afferent pathway carrying that signal has remained underspecified.
text.formatted: Classical facial-feedback accounts hold that facial motor activity contributes to emotion processing by feeding back into central affective systems <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">41</ref> , but the afferent pathway carrying that signal has remained underspecified.

text.text: ORIS supplies a candidate: the critical afferent signal is not musclebased proprioception but cutaneous mechanoreception conveyed by trigeminal pathways.

On this view emotion-related facial simulation depends on the integrity of a perioral surface-tension monitoring system, in which skin deformation rather than muscle contraction per se carries the relevant feedback.
A methodological implication follows directly.

Much of the facial-feedback literature has manipulated mimicry by constraining movement -holding a pen or chopstick between the teeth or lips, or paralyzing muscles pharmacologically -on the assumption that blocking the movement blocks the feedback.

ORIS reframes the operative variable: what the system reads is not movement as such but the pattern of cutaneous deformation, skin stretch and shear, that contraction imposes on the perioral sheet and that low-threshold mechanoreceptors (SA2 Ruffini, FA1 Meissner) transduce.
Constraining movement is therefore only an indirect and noisy proxy for that afferent signal.
It engages several muscles at once, alters effort and attention, and still leaves a residual uncontrolled skin deformation, since the constraint itself deforms the tissue.
This may be one reason facial-feedback effects on emotion recognition have proven difficult to replicate.

The model predicts instead that manipulations targeting skin deformation directly -directional skin stretch or taping, or low-frequency vibrotactile stimulation that injects noise into the mechanoreceptive signal, selectively deliverable given the paucity of Pacinian afferents in perioral skin -should isolate the afferent pathway more cleanly than movement constraint and yield more consistent effects on the accuracy with which observers recognize others' expressions.

This advantage holds only insofar as the deformation manipulation is decoupled from incidental motor consequences: contraction deforms skin, and externally imposed deformation can itself evoke reflexive motor adjustment, so the two factors are separable in principle but must be carefully dissociated in practice.
Evidence from congenital facial paralysis is broadly consistent with this account.
Möbius syndrome involves congenital hypoplasia or aplasia of the abducens (CN VI) and facial (CN VII) nuclei, with corresponding impairment of facial motor control.
Affected individuals show, to varying degrees, deficits in emotion recognition despite intact visual processing, pointing to disrupted simulation-based mechanisms 42, 43 .
text.formatted: Affected individuals show, to varying degrees, deficits in emotion recognition despite intact visual processing, pointing to disrupted simulation-based mechanisms <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">42,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">43</ref> .

text.text: From an ORIS perspective this deficit reflects not merely absent motor output but the failure to establish a functional afferent loop during development.

Without early coupling between facial movement and cutaneous feedback, the system never acquires the calibrated mapping between surface deformation and affective state that would normally support simulation.
The congenital case has an acquired counterpart that the model distinguishes sharply.
In acquired peripheral palsy, such as Bell's palsy or post-surgical paralysis, the deformation-to-affect mapping was calibrated normally in development and is disrupted only later.
ORIS therefore predicts a milder and potentially recoverable deficit, one that should track the status of the afferent loop rather than motor output alone.

This fits the mixed empirical picture: acquired palsy tends to slow emotion recognition and increase perceptual ambiguity while leaving accuracy largely preserved, consistent with compensation by an already-established mapping 44, 45 .

text.text: The contrast yields a testable prediction.

Congenital paralysis should produce a more fundamental simulation deficit than acquired paralysis of comparable motor severity, and in acquired cases recognition should recover with afferent rather than purely motor rehabilitation.
This interpretation extends to surgical rehabilitation.
Procedures such as gracilis free-muscle transfer can restore visible movement 46 but do not reinstate the original mechanoreceptive architecture (Belluardo et al., submitted).

text.text: The transferred muscle operates without an established sensory facial reference, which may limit its contribution to affective simulation even when motor output recovers.
Taken together, ORIS reframes the mechanism of facial feedback, shifting attention from motor execution to sensorimotor coupling and from muscle-centered accounts to skin-based afferent signaling.
The perspective generates testable predictions.

Selective disruption of perioral mechanoreception should impair emotion recognition even when overt facial movement is preserved, and interfering with cutaneous feedback during the observation of expressions should impair simulation-based processing.
This second prediction builds on evidence that facialexpression processing specifically engages the somatosensory channel: viewing facial expressions selectively modulates the somatosensory P300 47.
The ORIS model addresses feedback stabilization of voluntary perioral movements, not the motor programming of emotional displays.

Some experimental manipulations conducted under the facial feedback framework (e.g., constraining facial movement to test emotion effects) may inadvertently disrupt voluntary motor control rather than affective expression per se.
This distinction requires careful experimental dissociation in future work.
Three results would require revision of the model or a component of it -but first, two things the model does not claim.
It addresses motor stabilization of ongoing voluntary perioral movements; it says nothing about how movements are selected or initiated.

It also does not account for perceptual recognition of expressions in observers, except insofar as a companion perceptual account proposes that production and perception may share a representational substrate.

First, if the sparse spindles documented in the buccinator prove sufficient for the control precision observed, the primacy of CN V cutaneous mechanoreception would be downgraded to a modulatory role.
Second, if force transmission across the SMAS is diffuse rather than nodal, the modiolus may be anatomically prominent but mechanically peripheral.
Third, the most direct competing account is open-loop feedforward control: the motor system relies on highly practiced motor programs and corollary discharge, with no real-time afferent correction.
The perioral system executes voluntary movements with precision it anatomically should not be able to achieve.
Spindles are sparse or absent.
The facial nerve is purely efferent.
There are no joints.
And yet the motor system manages.

The ORIS model proposes that cutaneous mechanoreception via the trigeminal nerve is what makes this possible, organized around the orbicularis oris sphincter monitoring a surface tension equilibrium across the perioral sheet.

The orbicularis oris provides the circumferential tensile anchors; the modiolus transmits forces among converging directional muscles; SA2 Ruffini afferents are the most plausible candidates for encoding the distributed deformation pattern that constitutes the proposed controlled variable.
These proposals are grounded in established anatomy and physiology.
Their functional assembly into a working closed-loop architecture has not been demonstrated.
That is the gap.

The model's contribution at this stage is to organize the available evidence into a falsifiable architecture, one that specifies, for each of its three predictions, what result would confirm a specific component and what result would require revision.
A theoretical proposal that cannot say what would refute it is not yet science.
This one can.
Figure 1: The ORIS closed-loop control architecture.
Motor commands from cortical and brainstem centers travel via CN VII to sphincteric (orbicularis oris) and directional muscles, deforming the perioral sheet.

Cutaneous mechanoreceptors (SA1 Merkel, SA2 Ruffini, FA1 Meissner) transduce the resulting skin tension changes and transmit afferent signals via CN V. These signals drive corrective commands through a fast brainstem arc and a slower cortical loop.
Figure 2: Hub architecture of the perioral motor system.
The orbicularis oris encircles the oral aperture with circumferential fiber geometry, generating centripetal tension in all radial directions simultaneously.

Directional muscles -levator labii superioris, zygomaticus major, risorius, and depressor anguli oris -converge on the modiolus, the fibromuscular condensation at the labial commissure that serves as the primary force-transmission junction.
Arrows indicate the dominant force vectors of each muscle.
This arrangement is schematic; additional perioral muscles (buccinator, levator anguli oris, orbicularis oris inner and outer rings) are omitted for clarity.

The ORIS model proposes that the motor system regulates the spatial equilibrium of the tension field generated by the balance between sphincteric hub stabilization and directional muscle pull, rather than controlling individual muscles independently.
Figure 3.

Contrasting motor control architectures in the orofacial system and upper limb.The oral hub (upper panel) shows the orbicularis oris acting as a sphincteric tensile stabilizer, with directional muscles (e.g., risorius) producing antagonistic force vectors converging at the modiolus -a serial arrangement operating on a deformable surface without proprioceptive or visual feedback.

The arm (lower panel) illustrates the classical limb architecture: parallel muscles acting on a joint-based system with discrete degrees of freedom, supported by spindle-based proprioception and eventually visual monitoring.

Limb control stabilizes joint kinematics through spindle-based proprioception and an active gamma motor system that continuously adjusts spindle sensitivity during voluntary movement, preventing the limb from reverting toward a fixed mechanical equilibrium.
By contrast, the facial motor system lacks an equivalent gamma mechanism.
Consequently, voluntary perioral configurations are transient deviations from a preferred resting configuration rather than stable alternative equilibrium states.
The ORIS model therefore proposes that facial motor control stabilizes a distributed surface tension field around this default mechanical configuration.
Figure 4.
The ORIS closed-loop control architecture.
Motor commands from cortical and brainstem centers activate perioral muscles via CN VII, generating deformation of the perioral tension field.

Cutaneous mechanoreceptors in the facial skin detect resulting stretch and displacement and transmit afferent signals through CN V. These signals are integrated by fast brainstem and slower cortical pathways to generate corrective motor commands, stabilizing the spatial equilibrium of surface tension across the perioral sheet.
